source_text: Atque ita non transire ad posteros crimina generantium, quamvis ex eis nati sint, sicut nec filiorum ad parentes, qui de filiis suis nequaquam potuere generari. Ita igitur innocentiae nativitas sua officere non potest, sicut non potest obesse, cum non est.
pass_a_gloss: And so crimes of those generating do not pass to posterity, although they have been born from them, just as neither do sons' crimes pass to parents, who could by no means have been generated from their own sons. Thus therefore birth cannot stand in the way of innocence where it is, just as it cannot harm when it is not.

lemmas.lexica: LS nascor; Blaise of birth vs will

pass_b_english: And so parents’ crimes do not pass to their descendants, although those descendants were born from them, just as children’s crimes do not pass to their parents, who certainly could not have been born from their own children. Birth, then, can no more damage someone’s innocence where that birth exists than it can where it does not exist.

choices.why: Loaded word in Julian's Latin at this locus; English follows LS/Blaise range without copying NPNF.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

bible_refs.note: Continues the explicit argument from the law forbidding punishment of parents and children for one another’s sins.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
